strengths: The paper targets an important problem: learning methods that produce complete feasible MILP solutions rather than only partial assignments passed to a solver.

The proposed two-phase RL formulation is intuitive, separating feasibility discovery from objective improvement, and the paper gives a reasonably clear description of observations, actions, rewards, and the local-search inference loop.

The architecture combines a bipartite MILP graph encoder with a Transformer encoder, and the ablation table provides some evidence that the phase token, periodic embeddings, and separated phase heads matter on the authors' benchmark.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes useful diagrams/pseudocode that make the method easy to follow.
weaknesses: The empirical support is far too narrow for the central claims. Evaluation is limited to two synthetic random instance families with positive constraint coefficients, nonnegative all-integer variables, and small/moderate dimensions. There are no MIPLIB-style benchmarks, no real MILPs, no mixed continuous/integer cases, no binary-heavy cases, and no distribution shift tests.

The comparison set is weak. The paper compares mainly against Gurobi and two neural architecture variants, but omits relevant baselines such as feasibility pump variants, classical local search/rounding heuristics, the cited RL feasibility pump method, neural diving/primal heuristics, and simple nonlearned local-search baselines using the same LP-relaxation initialization.

The claim that the method solves MILPs end-to-end without traditional solvers is overstated: Algorithm 1 explicitly obtains an LP-relaxation solution and lower bound, which normally requires an LP/MILP optimization backend. The paper does not clarify what solver is used for this step or include its cost in a principled way.

The generated benchmark appears structurally easy and potentially favorable to the proposed method: A is nonnegative, b is constructed from a known feasible integer vector plus slack, bounds are fixed to x >= 0, and Gurobi solves all instances in under a second or essentially trivially within the time limit. This makes the reported roughly 1 percent gaps hard to interpret as evidence of a general MILP solver.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Key implementation details are missing, including layer sizes, number of GCN/Transformer layers, learning rates, optimizer settings, discounting/advantage formulation, episode step limits, local region size Delta, random seeds, hardware, training time, and whether code/data will be released.

The metrics and reporting are incomplete. Results are averaged over only 100 test instances with no variance, confidence intervals, per-instance scatter, failure analysis, or runtime/training-cost accounting. RP Gap is defined relative to the best method rather than certified optima, while Gurobi's status/gap handling is not explained.

Several methodological details are underspecified or questionable: the actor selects simultaneous +/-1/0 actions for every variable, but action factorization and exploration are not discussed; the critic is described as Q(S,A) but appears to receive only state embeddings; reward definitions sometimes use obj_t where obj_{t+1} seems intended; and the feasibility reward can reward improving already satisfied constraints rather than prioritizing violated ones.

Significance is currently limited. The method does not demonstrate scalability beyond 100 variables, does not outperform Gurobi, and only modestly improves over the authors' own MLP/CNN variants on one synthetic dataset.

Limitations are acknowledged only briefly. The paper notes restriction to all-integer variables and local-search limitations, but does not adequately discuss dependence on LP relaxation, lack of guarantees, benchmark narrowness, computational training cost, or poor applicability to standard mixed-integer instances.

No research ethics or broader impact discussion is provided. The ethical risk is likely low for this technical optimization paper, but the submission should still address potential deployment caveats for learned optimizers in high-stakes planning settings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: learning-based methods for MILP that can handle non-binary integer variables and produce complete feasible assignments rather than only partial primal hints.
The method is described at a reasonably high level, including the two-phase reward design, graph/Transformer architecture, and local-search inference procedure.
The authors include basic ablations for periodic embeddings, phase tokens, and separated actor/critic heads, which are useful for understanding the proposed architecture.
weaknesses: The central claim of an end-to-end ML-based MILP solver is not well supported. The inference algorithm explicitly obtains an LP relaxation solution and lower bound before search, so the method still relies on a traditional continuous optimization subroutine despite claims of eliminating reliance on traditional solvers.

The experimental benchmark is far too narrow and artificial for the paper's claims. All instances are synthetic, all variables are nonnegative integers, all constraint coefficients are positive, and the right-hand side is generated as Aξ+epsilon, which guarantees easy feasibility structure; no standard MILP benchmark, MIPLIB-style problem, real application, or diverse distribution is evaluated.

The comparison is weak. The only serious external baseline is Gurobi, which solves these small random instances essentially immediately; the remaining baselines are architectural variants rather than competitive MILP heuristics or learning-based primal methods. This does not establish significance over prior work.

The feasibility results are not convincing because the generated problems have an obvious feasible point x=0 under Ax<=b with b positive and x>=0. Reporting 100/100 feasible rate and subsecond first feasible times is therefore not strong evidence of solving difficult MILPs.

The RP Gap metric and results are problematic. RP Gap is defined relative to the best objective found across all methods, so at least one method should have 0 by construction, yet Table 2 reports Gurobi at 0.01 on D100*50. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the evaluation and reporting.

The method has no optimality guarantee and uses a local search with fixed +/-1 actions, but the paper makes broad solver-level claims. Scalability to larger variable ranges, mixed continuous/integer variables, equality constraints, negative coefficients, and harder feasible regions is not demonstrated.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including model sizes, learning rates, rollout lengths, discounting/advantage estimation details, local region size Delta, step limits, seeds, hardware, training time, and whether code/data will be released.

The presentation is understandable but sometimes overclaims. The manuscript frames the contribution as a foundation for ML-driven solvers, yet the evidence is limited to two small synthetic settings where Gurobi is already effectively instantaneous.

The limitations section acknowledges continuous variables and local-search limitations, but does not sufficiently discuss the narrow synthetic distribution, the trivial feasible point, dependence on LP relaxation, weak baselines, or lack of evidence on standard MILP benchmarks.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: learning-based solution methods for MILPs that produce complete feasible assignments rather than only partial primal-heuristic predictions handed to a solver. The focus on non-binary integer variables is useful, since much prior ML-for-MIP work emphasizes binary decisions.

The proposed formulation is conceptually coherent. The two-phase RL design separates feasibility-seeking from objective improvement, and the local-search interpretation with increase/decrease/hold actions is intuitive and well matched to integer variables.

The architecture is reasonably motivated: a bipartite MILP graph captures local variable-constraint structure, while the Transformer encoder is used to model longer-range interactions among variables. The ablation study on periodic embeddings, phase token, and phase-specific actor/critic heads supports the importance of the main architectural choices.

Empirically, the method consistently finds feasible solutions on the reported test instances and achieves competitive objective quality on the two synthetic datasets, including matching Gurobi on the small setting and outperforming MLP/CNN variants on the larger setting.

The paper is generally readable, with clear figures, pseudocode, and an honest discussion that local search does not guarantee global optimality and that the present work only handles all-integer MILPs rather than general mixed continuous/integer problems.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the solver-level claims. Results are shown only on two synthetic random-instance families, with the larger case being 100 variables and 50 constraints. There are no standard MILP benchmark sets, no real application instances, and no tests of distribution shift or scalability to substantially larger/harder problems.

The feasibility claim is weakened by the instance generator. With nonnegative variables, positive constraint coefficients, and positive right-hand sides constructed as Aξ + ε, the all-zero solution is feasible for every generated instance. Thus finding a feasible solution is structurally easy in this benchmark, and FR/FFST do not convincingly demonstrate that the RL method solves the hard feasibility issues motivating the paper.

The comparison to Gurobi is not very informative. Gurobi solves all instances essentially immediately and obtains the best or nearly best objective. The paper does not report wall-clock training cost, inference step counts, hardware, exact Gurobi settings, or objective values, so it is difficult to assess practical competitiveness.

The claim that the method eliminates reliance on traditional solvers is overstated. The search algorithm uses the LP relaxation to obtain the initial solution and lower bound, which normally requires an optimization solver. This is less severe than delegating the remaining MILP subproblem, but it should be acknowledged more carefully.

Important reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including random seeds, network widths/depths, optimizer settings, learning rates, rollout lengths, local region size Δ, step limits, termination thresholds, number of training instances seen, hardware, and variance across runs. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

The baselines are limited. MLP/CNN variants are useful architectural controls, but the paper does not compare against simple local search, feasibility pump variants, learned primal heuristics adapted to these instances, or non-learned rounding/repair heuristics. Given that x=0 is always feasible, stronger simple baselines are especially important.

Some methodological choices need more justification. The phase-2 reward gives positive reward to infeasible solutions inside the objective interval and no penalty to feasible solutions outside it, which may be reasonable but is not theoretically analyzed. The action step size is fixed to 1, which may limit scalability for variables with large domains.

The presentation occasionally overclaims significance, especially phrases such as solving MILPs end-to-end based solely on ML and establishing a foundation for eliminating traditional solvers. The actual contribution is better characterized as an initial learned local-search method for a restricted all-integer synthetic MILP setting.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of many learned MILP heuristics: feasibility and non-binary integer variables. Framing solution improvement as a two-phase RL/local-search process is a reasonable and potentially useful direction.

The method is described with enough algorithmic detail to understand the main mechanics: observation/action design, feasibility and objective rewards, phase switching, local search behavior, and the GNN/Transformer policy architecture. The appendices include pseudocode and instance-generation details.

The ablations are directionally informative: the Transformer, message passing, phase token, separated layers, and periodic embeddings are each tested, and the results suggest that the architectural choices are not arbitrary.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is far too narrow for the paper's broad claims about solving MILPs. All experiments use synthetic all-integer instances with nonnegative constraints, nonnegative variables, negative objective coefficients, and feasible right-hand sides constructed from small random integer vectors. This is a very special and relatively benign family, not representative of general MILP structure, mixed continuous/integer variables, equality constraints, negative coefficients, complex presolve behavior, or real benchmarks such as MIPLIB.

The baseline comparison is weak. Gurobi solves all reported instances in under one second, so the paper does not demonstrate advantage over established solvers on hard instances. Existing learned primal heuristics are excluded rather than adapted or compared on settings they can handle, and the LS baseline is initialized using the proposed method's phase-1 solution, making interpretation difficult.

The central claim of a solver that does not rely on off-the-shelf solvers is overstated. The algorithm explicitly calls an LP relaxation step to obtain the initial solution and lower bound, and the experiments use Gurobi to compute best-known values. This may be acceptable as a component, but the manuscript should state the dependence clearly and evaluate its cost and failure modes.

The reported near-optimality is not very convincing. The gap is measured against best-known values from the compared methods, including Gurobi, but the paper does not provide optimality certificates for the learned solver, statistical variability, confidence intervals, seed sensitivity, or detailed per-instance behavior. Some reported Gurobi gaps are nonzero despite Gurobi being used with a longer time limit for BKS, which needs clarification.

Scalability remains unresolved. The policy uses a Transformer over variables/constraints and the action space changes all variables simultaneously, but the largest test has only 300 variables and 100 constraints, with small generated solution magnitudes. There is no analysis of memory/time scaling, training cost, or performance on larger or more difficult MILPs.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives pseudocode and some implementation details, but key hyperparameters such as step limits, warmup, grace period, local-region size, random seeds, training time, model sizes, and evaluation protocols are under-specified or scattered. No code or trained models are promised.

The limitations and ethics discussion is essentially absent. While the topic has limited direct ethical risk, the paper should explicitly discuss limitations such as lack of guarantees, narrow distributional evaluation, solver dependence for relaxation/BKS, and risks of deploying infeasible or suboptimal decisions in high-stakes optimization settings.

Presentation is mostly clear, but several claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially phrases such as full end-to-end solver, achieves near-optimal solutions, and opens the door to a unified LP solver. The theoretical proposition is true but elementary and does not provide a meaningful guarantee for the learned search procedure.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: learning-based methods for MILP that can produce complete feasible assignments for integer variables, rather than only partial assignments passed to a solver.

The proposed two-phase reward design is clearly motivated around feasibility first and objective improvement second, and the manuscript gives pseudocode and enough high-level architectural detail to understand the intended algorithm.
The experiments include ablations over architectural components and the toward-optimal bias parameter, which helps isolate some design choices within the proposed system.
weaknesses: The central claim of a standalone full end-to-end MILP solver is not well supported. Algorithm 1 explicitly calls an LP relaxation routine to obtain x0 and objr, but the implementation of this relaxation is not specified and likely relies on a conventional solver. This undercuts the claim of avoiding off-the-shelf solvers, especially because objr is essential to the reward and search strategy.

There appears to be a serious soundness issue around integrality. The algorithm initializes x0 from the LP relaxation and then applies integer-valued increments/decrements. If x0 is fractional, these moves preserve the fractional parts and cannot generally reach an integer-feasible solution. The feasibility reward checks linear constraints and bounds but does not appear to penalize violation of integrality. This is a fundamental gap for a paper whose main focus is integer MILPs.

The evaluation is far too narrow and artificial. All instances come from one synthetic generator with positive A, nonnegative variables, and b constructed from a sampled feasible point; Gurobi solves all test cases in under one second. This does not demonstrate usefulness on realistic MILIB/MIPLIB-style benchmarks, harder structured MILPs, mixed continuous/integer problems, equality constraints, negative coefficients, or varied sparsity/scale regimes.

The comparisons are weak. The paper does not compare against standard primal heuristics such as feasibility pump, SCIP/Gurobi heuristics under matched time budgets, or relevant neural primal methods adapted to these instances. Reporting that the learned method finds feasible solutions quickly is not convincing when Gurobi already solves the instances essentially instantly.

The runtime evidence is misleading. The solver is allowed up to 100 seconds, while Gurobi reaches optimality or near-optimality in less than one second on every dataset. The table emphasizes first-feasible time rather than time-to-best objective, training cost, or wall-clock time needed to match solver quality.

The reported gaps are relative to best-known values across methods, but Gurobi is also run for 600 seconds to define BKS. The relationship between the 100-second evaluation, the 600-second BKS run, and the listed Gurobi gaps is confusing; if Gurobi solves the instances in under one second, the nonzero Gurobi gaps on larger datasets need explanation.

The theoretical component is very limited. Proposition 1 is essentially the standard fact that the LP relaxation objective is a lower bound for minimization MILPs; it does not justify the RL reward design beyond a loose heuristic and provides no guarantee of feasibility, convergence, or optimality.

The architecture has scalability concerns that are not addressed. The Transformer attends globally over graph-derived tokens, and the variable embedding appears to include c|A^T, whose dimensionality grows with the number of constraints. This conflicts with claims of scalability and is only tested up to 300 variables and 100 constraints.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix lists some hyperparameters and GitHub sources, but there are no seeds, variance/error bars, training times, code release statement, model sizes, detailed stopping criteria behavior, or enough information to reproduce all tables reliably.

Limitations and ethics are not adequately discussed. The paper does not clearly acknowledge the dependence on LP relaxation, the synthetic-only evaluation, lack of optimality guarantees, possible failure modes on infeasible/unbounded instances, or the risks of using approximate MILP solvers in operational decision-making contexts.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored direction: full-solution learning for MILPs with non-binary integer variables, rather than only binary-variable partial assignments handed to a solver.

The RL formulation is reasonably concrete, with a two-phase reward design for first reaching feasibility and then improving incumbent solutions, plus a search strategy tied to LP-relaxation lower bounds.
The architecture is well motivated: combining local bipartite message passing with a Transformer encoder is a plausible way to capture both constraint-local and longer-range variable interactions.

The experiments show encouraging feasibility behavior on the tested synthetic instances: the proposed method achieves 100% feasible rate in the main tables and sub-1-second first-feasible-solution times.
The paper includes useful ablations over Transformer encoder, MPNN, periodic embeddings, separated layers, and phase token, and provides several implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central claims are much broader than the evidence supports. The experiments use a narrow synthetic integer-only MILP family with positive sparse A, nonnegative variables, negative objective coefficients, and constructed feasible right-hand sides. This does not substantiate claims about solving general MILPs after standard-form transformations, mixed continuous/integer variables, equality constraints, negative coefficients, or realistic industrial instances.

The method appears to rely on LP relaxation in Algorithm 1 to obtain x0 and objr, likely via an external optimizer, while the paper repeatedly claims not to rely on off-the-shelf solvers. This needs clarification and weakens the claimed full end-to-end solver framing.

The comparison to Gurobi does not establish practical advantage: Gurobi finds feasible solutions in under one second and optimal or near-optimal solutions on all reported datasets, while the proposed method has nonzero gaps on larger instances. The paper does not report training cost, total inference time to best solution, or wall-clock tradeoffs relative to standard solver heuristics.

Baselines are limited. The paper omits strong relevant solver heuristics and learning-based approaches adapted through reasonable encodings, and the local-search baseline is initialized by the proposed RL agent, making it hard to isolate the contribution of phase-2 search.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and software are listed, but there is no code release statement, random seed protocol, variance/error bars, or enough detail to confidently reproduce the training dynamics and generated datasets.

The theoretical contribution is modest: Proposition 1 is essentially the standard LP-relaxation lower-bound property and does not provide guarantees for the RL search, feasibility, convergence, or optimality.

The limitations and ethics discussion is largely absent. The paper should explicitly discuss restricted problem distributions, lack of optimality guarantees, dependence on relaxation solving, compute/training cost, and failure modes on out-of-distribution or infeasible/unbounded MILPs.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical gap in learned primal heuristics: independently producing feasible ILP solutions, including non-binary integer variables, rather than only proposing partial assignments for a solver.

The paper gives a reasonably complete algorithmic description, including the RL state/action/reward design, variable-selection strategy, architecture components, pseudocode, benchmark generation details, and hyperparameters.

Empirical results are promising on the reported synthetic benchmarks: RL-SPH reaches 100% feasibility in all tables, improves primal gap/integral over several SCIP start heuristics, and the ablations suggest that the transformer encoder and reward context contribute materially.
The work is positioned clearly relative to learned predict-and-search methods and classical start primal heuristics, and the focus on feasibility is a useful contribution direction.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not sound. Proposition 1 assumes persistent positive constraint-reward improvement and zero bound violations, which is essentially assuming the hard part of reaching feasibility; it does not show that the learned policy will choose such actions. The proof also jumps from a monotone bounded sequence to finite-time feasibility without a justified finite-time argument. Thus claims of a theoretical feasibility guarantee are overstated.

The experimental comparison to classical start heuristics is not fully convincing. SCIP heuristics are run with presolving and branching disabled, each baseline is enabled alone with default settings, and RL-SPH is allowed to run until all baselines terminate despite using a GPU-trained policy. This does not cleanly establish superiority under matched computational budgets or realistic solver settings.

The metrics and reporting can be misleading. PG and PI are averaged only over instances where a feasible solution is found, so methods with very low feasibility rates can appear excellent, e.g. Diving/RENS on SC have 0 PG despite 1%/3% feasibility. The headline 44x improvement depends on this evaluation design and selected baselines.

The solver-combination experiment is narrow: it evaluates only IS and NBI, PAS is inapplicable to NBI, and RL-SPH+S uses a custom fixing scheme based on feasible solutions from the first five seconds. This leaves unclear whether the method improves modern solver performance broadly across MILP classes.

The benchmarks are mostly synthetic and structurally limited. The only non-binary integer benchmark is generated from a specific random construction with nonnegative A and unbounded upper bounds, so evidence for real-world mixed-integer problems, equality constraints, mixed signs, variable bounds, and heterogeneous industrial MILPs is limited.

Reproducibility is partial. The paper reports environment, hyperparameters, and source repositories for components/baselines, but does not clearly commit to releasing the RL-SPH implementation, trained models, generated instances, or exact seeds. Given the sensitivity of RL training and solver heuristics, this is a material gap.

The architecture/method has several heuristic choices whose robustness is underexplored, including p=q=log2 n variable selection, reward scaling, rollback behavior in phase2, alpha selection, and initialization. Ablations cover only a subset of components and only two datasets for the main architecture table.

Presentation is generally clear but sometimes overclaims: phrases such as 'guaranteed to discover a feasible solution' and 'theoretically guaranteeing feasibility' are not supported by the provided analysis or experiments. The paper would be stronger if framed as an empirical learned heuristic rather than as a guaranteed feasibility method.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: learned primal heuristics that can independently produce feasible ILP solutions, including non-binary integer variables, would be useful if convincingly demonstrated.
The method is described in reasonable detail, with reward definitions, variable-selection pseudocode, training pseudocode, and implementation hyperparameters in the appendix.

The empirical results suggest the proposed heuristic can find feasible solutions on the tested generated benchmarks, and the ablations indicate that the transformer encoder and reward context matter for performance.
weaknesses: The main theoretical claim is not sound. Proposition 1 assumes positive feasibility improvement and no bound violations at every step, which is essentially the hard part, and the proof only shows monotone increase of a violation measure bounded by zero, not finite-time feasibility. The text then overstates this as a guarantee that a well-trained agent discovers feasible solutions.

The experimental comparison is not convincing. In Table 1, SCIP baselines are run with presolving and branching disabled and only one heuristic family enabled, while RL-SPH is a learned GPU-based method allowed to run until all baselines terminate. This does not establish superiority over practical solver behavior or well-tuned primal heuristics.

The evaluation protocol has several biases and ambiguities. PG and PI are averaged only over instances where a feasible solution is found, which can make methods with very low feasibility rate look artificially good. PI is defined as a sum over timesteps rather than a time integral, but methods have very different computational costs per step. Training and LP initialization costs are not consistently accounted for.

The claimed support for general integer variables is weak. The main start-heuristic comparison in Table 1 omits the NBI benchmark entirely; NBI appears only in Table 2 against SCIP, with PAS marked N/A, and the generated NBI distribution is synthetic with nonnegative coefficients and an easily constructed feasible structure.

The solver-combination experiment is too narrow to support the broad claims. Table 2 uses only IS and NBI under a 50-second limit, compares to default SCIP and PAS+SCIP, and uses an additional variable-fixing procedure based on RL-SPH solutions from the first five seconds. It is unclear how much of the gain comes from the proposed RL policy versus this downstream fixing strategy.

The paper under-engages with closely related RL-based feasibility-pump and MIP heuristic work, including Qi et al. (2021), despite using it for NBI generation. This weakens the originality claim that RL-SPH is the first to explicitly learn feasibility for ILP.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript lists hardware, software, hyperparameters, and external code sources, but does not appear to provide its own implementation or exact instance seeds/splits. The method also depends on stochastic training and selection, yet the reporting lacks multiple training seeds or confidence intervals over independent runs.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially 'theoretically guaranteeing feasibility,' 'naturally generalizes beyond binary variables,' and the 44x/2.3x headline results. There are also minor inconsistencies, such as saying two experiments and then listing three, and a duplicated p parameter where q is intended in the appendix.

strengths: The paper tackles an important limitation of learning-based primal heuristics: independently producing feasible solutions, including for non-binary integer variables. This is a meaningful and useful direction for ML-for-CO and differentiates the work from predict-and-search methods that still rely on a solver to repair feasibility.

The proposed RL formulation is concrete and reasonably well motivated: observations include solution, feasibility residuals, and objective; rewards separate pre-feasibility and post-feasibility behavior; and the search strategy selects variables based on violated or low-risk constraints. The Transformer-based GNN and ablations provide evidence that architecture choices, especially global attention, matter.

Empirical results are promising. RL-SPH achieves 100% feasibility across the reported benchmarks, substantially improves primal gap/integral against SCIP start heuristics in Table 1, and improves early solving performance when combined with SCIP in Table 2. The inclusion of a synthetic non-binary integer benchmark is especially relevant to the paper’s main claim.

Reproducibility is better than average: the paper specifies datasets, generator sources, solver version, hardware/software environment, hyperparameters, training time, and links to major code components/baselines.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee is overstated. Proposition 1 assumes persistent positive constraint-reward improvement and no bound violations, but these are precisely the hard conditions the learned policy must achieve. A monotone increasing sequence bounded by 0 also need not reach 0 in finite time without additional discreteness/step-size arguments. Thus the paper does not really establish that a trained agent is guaranteed to find a feasible solution.

The evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. Four of five benchmarks are binary, and the only non-binary integer benchmark is synthetic with a specific generation process. There is no evaluation on standard heterogeneous MILP libraries such as MIPLIB or on mixed binary/integer/continuous models, so the claim of broadly addressing real-world ILPs remains only partially supported.

Baseline fairness and reporting need strengthening. RL-SPH uses GPU inference and learned offline training while SCIP heuristics are run under modified solver settings with presolving and branching disabled. Training cost is mostly excluded from comparisons, and Table 1 lets RL-SPH run until all baselines terminate, which may not correspond to equal wall-clock budgets. The solver-combined experiment is limited to two datasets and a 50s budget.

Some metrics can obscure failures. PG and PI are averaged only over instances where a feasible solution is found, so methods with very low feasibility rates can appear artificially strong, e.g. zero PG for Diving/RENS on SC despite 1%-3% FR. This is disclosed, but the headline average improvement depends on comparing only methods with 100% FR and should be interpreted cautiously.

The presentation is generally clear but has inconsistencies and minor issues: the experiments section says two experiments and then lists three; the appendix states the number of neighboring variables p=log2 n instead of q=log2 n; and several reward cases/equations are hard to parse, making it difficult to verify implementation fidelity from the paper alone.

Limitations and ethics are only lightly treated. The paper acknowledges possible suboptimality from fixing variables but does not discuss failure modes, compute/environmental costs, deployment risks for optimization decisions, or robustness under distribution shift. These are not fatal, but they reduce confidence in practical applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for learning-based ILP heuristics: producing feasible solutions without delegating feasibility recovery to an external solver. Framing the method as a start primal heuristic is useful and clearly distinguishes it from one-shot prediction methods and solver-assisted predict-and-search approaches.

The proposed RL-SPH design is coherent: a two-phase reward, feasibility-aware variable selection, and a compact Graph Transformer policy over selected variables are well motivated for iterative repair/search. The method also handles non-binary integer variables, which is a meaningful extension beyond much prior E2EPH work focused on binaries.

The empirical evaluation is broad by ML-for-CO standards. It compares against SCIP start-heuristic families, feasibility pump, RENS, rounding/diving variants, and learned baselines such as PAS, DDIM, and DiffILO; it reports feasibility rate, first feasible time, primal gap, and primal integral across five benchmark families.

The results are promising: RL-SPH obtains 100% feasibility on all main benchmarks and often substantially improves primal gap/integral over baselines with 100% feasibility. The ablations support the importance of feasibility-aware selection and Transformer components.

Reproducibility details are relatively strong: the paper gives dataset sizes, generation procedures, hyperparameters, training times, model sizes, software/hardware environment, and baseline heuristic families. The appendices include additional generalization, presolve, solver-integration, sensitivity, and qualitative analyses.
weaknesses: The theoretical claim of reward-feasibility alignment is overstated. Proposition 1 essentially assumes the desired monotone feasibility improvement condition, Rt,const > 0 with no bound violations at every step, and then proves eventual feasibility under discreteness. This does not establish that the learned policy will satisfy the condition, nor does it provide a guarantee for RL-SPH. The central feasibility claim is therefore empirical rather than theoretically guaranteed.

The generality claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Most main benchmarks are synthetic and structurally regular; the MIPLIB experiment uses only 17 instances, appears selective, and shows poor incumbent quality on several cases such as scpk4 and bppc8-02. Cross-problem generalization is also mixed: models trained on IS fail on MVC and vice versa, requiring joint training.

Baseline fairness is not fully settled. SCIP start heuristics are evaluated with presolving and branching disabled to isolate heuristic behavior, while RL-SPH can use LP initialization, GPU inference, learned offline training, and additional search design. This is a defensible experimental choice, but it weakens conclusions about practical dominance over solver machinery unless wall-clock accounting and integration settings are made more uniform.

The comparison to learned E2EPH baselines may understate their potential because the paper mainly uses released/default configurations, while noting that some methods are sensitive to benchmark-specific tuning. Conversely, RL-SPH is tuned through architectural and search choices developed for this setting, so the claim of robust superiority should be tempered.

Some metrics can obscure failure modes. PG, PI, and FT are averaged only over instances where a feasible solution is found, so methods with low feasibility can appear strong on the surviving cases; the paper does report FR separately, but some claims based on averaged improvements should be interpreted cautiously.

The method still relies on nontrivial instance-specific training distributions and has computational bottlenecks in variable selection, O(mn), plus limited demonstrated performance on dense or very large real-world ILPs. The limitations section mentions these issues, but the main text sometimes presents RL-SPH as closer to a unified solver than the evidence justifies.

The ethics/impact statement is generic and does not discuss possible downstream risks of optimization systems, such as resource allocation harms or misuse in high-stakes automated planning. This is not a major blocker for this technical contribution, but the treatment is minimal.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored issue for learning-based ILP heuristics: obtaining feasible solutions without delegating feasibility repair to a full solver.

The proposed RL-SPH framework is reasonably coherent at a high level, combining phase-specific rewards, local search over selected variables, and a graph-transformer policy. The feasibility-aware variable selection is simple and appears practically useful.

The empirical section is broad in surface area: five synthetic benchmark families, comparisons to SCIP start-primal heuristic families and several learning-based baselines, ablations, initialization studies, and some distribution/size/density shift tests.
The reported results on the main synthetic benchmarks are promising, especially the consistent 100% feasibility rate and strong primal gap/primal integral numbers relative to the selected baselines.
Implementation details are more complete than average, including dataset sizes, hyperparameters, training times, model sizes, hardware, and baseline heuristic families.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is weak. Proposition 1 assumes the desired monotone feasibility progress, namely Rt,const > 0 and Rt,bound = 0 at all infeasible steps, and then proves feasibility follows. This is essentially a conditional statement that if the search keeps improving constraint violation without bound violations, it eventually becomes feasible; it does not establish that the reward or learned policy will do so. The manuscript repeatedly presents this as “theoretical reward-feasibility alignment,” which overstates what is shown.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness concerns. SCIP baselines are run with presolving and branching disabled to isolate heuristics, while RL-SPH relies on learned GPU inference and often LP initialization. The stopping rule is also unusual: RL-SPH, which has no native termination condition, runs until baselines finish. This makes wall-clock and primal integral comparisons hard to interpret.

The paper’s claims about generalization are overstated. In cross-problem transfer, a model trained only on IS obtains 0% feasibility on MVC and vice versa. The joint model works on those two families, but that is much weaker than broad generalization. The MIPLIB appendix contains only 17 selected instances, and RL-SPH is often far from BKS and sometimes much worse than RHF, e.g. scpk4 and bppc8-02.

The main benchmarks are mostly synthetic and structurally narrow. The NBI benchmark is an unbounded multidimensional knapsack-style construction with positive resource coefficients and negative objective coefficients; success there does not demonstrate robust handling of general non-binary ILPs.

The comparison to learning-based baselines is not fully convincing. Several baselines are excluded, inapplicable, or evaluated under configurations that differ substantially from their original settings. The paper uses these failures to make broad claims about E2EPH feasibility, but the evidence is not strong enough for that conclusion.

Some reported metrics can obscure failures. PG, PI, and FT are averaged only over instances where a feasible solution is found, so methods with poor feasibility can still appear competitive on quality/time metrics. The paper does report FR, but the narrative sometimes mixes these quantities in ways that favor the proposed method.

The ablations support that the hand-crafted feasibility-aware selection and transformer components help, but they do not disentangle how much of the gain comes from RL versus deterministic repair/local-search structure. A stronger non-learned version of the same variable-selection/search procedure is missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript cites external code for baselines and components, but does not clearly state that RL-SPH code, trained models, exact generated datasets, and scripts will be released. Given the sensitivity of SCIP/Gurobi settings, random seeds, and generated instances, this is a material concern.

The limitations and ethics treatment is thin. Important caveats about solver comparison fairness, poor cross-problem transfer, MIPLIB underperformance, and scaling bottlenecks are mostly relegated to appendices or framed optimistically; the impact statement is boilerplate.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and concrete bottleneck in learning-based ILP heuristics: obtaining feasible solutions independently rather than relying on an external solver to repair infeasible ML predictions. The focus on start primal heuristics and non-binary integer variables is well motivated and useful.

The proposed RL-SPH framework is technically coherent: the action space preserves integrality, the two-phase reward separates feasibility discovery from incumbent improvement, and the feasibility-aware variable selection gives the RL agent a tractable local search interface.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall. The paper compares against SCIP start-primal-heuristic families and representative E2EPH methods, reports feasibility rate, primal gap, primal integral, and first-feasible time, and includes ablations, cross-problem tests, distribution/size/density shifts, MIPLIB instances, and solver integration.

The results are strong for the stated goal. RL-SPH reaches 100% feasibility on all five main benchmarks, often improves primal gap and primal integral over baselines, and demonstrates useful behavior from random, LP, and learned initializations.
Presentation is generally clear, with helpful algorithms, architectural diagrams, and appendices that explain benchmark generation, hyperparameters, baseline setup, and additional experiments.
weaknesses: The theoretical claim of reward-feasibility alignment is weaker than the wording suggests. Proposition 1 essentially proves convergence under the strong assumption that constraint violation strictly improves at every step while bounds remain satisfied; it does not show that the learned policy will satisfy these assumptions or that reward maximization reliably implies feasibility in general ILPs.

The strongest empirical claims are still mostly on generated benchmark distributions. The MIPLIB experiment is a valuable sanity check, but it uses only 17 instances, sometimes performs substantially worse than RHF, and does not establish broad general-purpose ILP reliability.

Some comparisons may favor RL-SPH through framing and implementation choices. Baseline SCIP heuristics are isolated with presolving and branching disabled in the main SPH comparison, while RL-SPH uses a GPU-trained policy and custom stopping tied to baseline completion; this is reasonable for studying heuristic behavior but limits conclusions about practical solver competitiveness.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete from the manuscript alone. Many implementation details are provided, including hyperparameters and hardware, but I did not see a clear release of the authors' RL-SPH code or trained models, which matters for a relatively complex RL system.

The method's limitations are acknowledged in the appendix but somewhat understated in the main text: cross-problem single-task generalization fails, performance can degrade on very large or structurally different instances, and hyperparameters such as neighbor ratio can matter substantially.

Ethical risks appear low for this optimization-method paper, but there is little explicit discussion of research ethics or downstream misuse/energy considerations. This is not a major concern, but a short statement would improve completeness.
